lessons.title: Query an actual database
lessons.concept: A relational table has rows and named columns. SELECT chooses columns, WHERE filters rows, and ORDER BY makes result order explicit. sqlite3 can create a temporary in-memory database for repeatable practice without installing a database server.

import sqlite3

lessons.task: Write sql_affordable(rows, budget). rows contains [title, price] pairs. Create SQLite table games(title TEXT, price INTEGER), insert rows with parameters, and query titles with price <= budget, sorted by title. Return a list of strings.
lessons.name: sql_affordable
lessons.solution:
def sql_affordable(rows, budget):
    import sqlite3
    con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
    try:
        con.execute("CREATE TABLE games(title TEXT, price INTEGER)")
        con.executemany("INSERT INTO games VALUES (?, ?)", rows)
        return [row[0] for row in con.execute("SELECT title FROM games WHERE price <= ? ORDER BY title", (budget,))]
    finally:
        con.close()

Bind budget with a ? placeholder; fetch results and extract each title.

lessons.title: Join related tables
lessons.concept: A join relates rows through matching keys. A LEFT JOIN preserves every left-side row, even when no right-side record exists. One-to-many joins can multiply rows, so group deliberately and inspect counts rather than assuming each output row represents one entity.
lessons.example:
SELECT g.title, s.minutes
FROM games g LEFT JOIN sessions s ON s.game_id = g.id;
lessons.task: Write sql_library(games, sessions). games is [id, title]; sessions is [game_id, minutes]. Create both tables and return [title, total_minutes] lists sorted by title. Include games without sessions with total 0. Game IDs are unique.
lessons.name: sql_library
lessons.solution:
def sql_library(games, sessions):
    import sqlite3
    con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
    try:
        con.execute("CREATE TABLE games(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT)")
        con.execute("CREATE TABLE sessions(game_id INTEGER, minutes INTEGER)")
        con.executemany("INSERT INTO games VALUES (?, ?)", games)
        con.executemany("INSERT INTO sessions VALUES (?, ?)", sessions)
        query = "SELECT g.title, COALESCE(SUM(s.minutes), 0) FROM games g LEFT JOIN sessions s ON g.id = s.game_id GROUP BY g.id, g.title ORDER BY g.title"
        return [list(row) for row in con.execute(query)]
    finally:
        con.close()
hints: Start with games and LEFT JOIN sessions.
Use COALESCE(SUM(...), 0) to replace the missing total.
lessons.extension: Add a foreign key and reject sessions for nonexistent games. Explain INNER JOIN vs LEFT JOIN with one small example.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: parameters protect the query

def sql_lookup(titles, wanted):

    finally:

lessons.title: Checkpoint: prioritize tasks
lessons.concept: A min-heap keeps the smallest item ready without fully sorting after every insertion. heapq works on a list. Tuples compare left to right, which can encode priority then a stable sequence number. Understand your tie policy before choosing the heap entries.
lessons.example:

heap = []
heapq.heappush(heap, (2, "task"))
lessons.task: Write priority_order(tasks). tasks contains [name, priority] pairs. Use a heap to return names in priority ascending order, preserving original order for equal priorities.
lessons.name: priority_order
lessons.solution:
def priority_order(tasks):
    import heapq
    heap = [(priority, index, name) for index, (name, priority) in enumerate(tasks)]
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    return [heapq.heappop(heap)[2] for _ in range(len(heap))]
hints: Include the original index as a tie-breaker before the name.
Heap entries can be (priority, index, name).

def max_profit(prices):
    lowest = float('inf')
    best = 0
    for p in prices:

        best = max(best, p - lowest)
    return best

lessons.name: product_except_self
lessons.solution:
def product_except_self(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    out = [1] * n
    left = 1
    for i in range(n):
        out[i] = left
        left *= nums[i]
    right = 1
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        out[i] *= right
        right *= nums[i]
    return out

import sqlite3

def transfer(start_a, start_b, amount):
    db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
    db.execute("CREATE TABLE accounts (name TEXT, balance INTEGER)")
    db.executemany("INSERT INTO accounts VALUES (?, ?)", [("a", start_a), ("b", start_b)])
    db.commit()
    db.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - ? WHERE name = 'a'", (amount,))
    db.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + ? WHERE name = 'b'", (amount,))
    balance = db.execute("SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE name = 'a'").fetchone()[0]
    if balance < 0:
        db.rollback()
    else:
        db.commit()
    rows = db.execute("SELECT balance FROM accounts ORDER BY name").fetchall()
    return [row[0] for row in rows]
